label: Place
name: Guadeloupe
summary:
Guadeloupe is an overseas department and region of the French Republic in the Caribbean, consisting of six inhabited islands including Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre. With 400,000 people, Guadeloupe is legally and constitutionally part of France — an outermost region of the European Union — rather than a colony or overseas territory.

Columbus reached Guadeloupe in 1493 on his second voyage. The indigenous Kalinago (Island Caribs) resisted Spanish and French colonization for over a century before French permanent settlement was established in 1635. The subsequent plantation economy, built on African enslaved labor, produced sugar that made Guadeloupe one of the most profitable islands in the Caribbean by the 18th century. The British seized Guadeloupe during the Seven Years' War (1759–1763) and at the 1763 Peace of Paris, France controversially chose to keep Guadeloupe rather than Canada — a decision that profoundly shaped North American history.

The French Revolution brought abolition of slavery (1794), reinstated by Napoleon in 1802, triggering a revolt in which Guadeloupean Louis Delgrès led a famous last stand rather than surrender to restored slavery — dying in an explosion at Matouba with 300 followers. Final abolition came in 1848 under Victor Schoelcher. Guadeloupe became a French département (not a colony) in 1946, integrating fully into metropolitan France's social and political structures.

Full French citizenship and EU membership (since 1946) giving Guadeloupe a unique post-colonial status
